heavy borrowings sank its shares and bonds last week, dragging rival Nebius

has walked away from a UK lease with Nscale over delays connecting the project to the electricity grid. While the London-based group has said the setback will not impact its relationship with the software giant that is one of its two largest tenants, the glitch raises further questions about the ability of chip landlords to deliver vast infrastructure.

Investors’ misgivings about the companies collectively known as neoclouds have not appeared out of thin air. Their reliance on long-term contracts with a handful of customers is well established. For example, Microsoft and Anthropic account for some 85% of Nscale's $103 billion of future contracts. Data centre developers are also heavily dependent on suppliers and utilities – not to mention planning authorities and local politicians – to get facilities up and running on schedule. Some contracts allow customers to walk away in the event of major construction snags. It’s therefore no surprise that Microsoft axed its agreement for Nscale’s data centre in Loughton when it became clear the facility faced energy supply delays.

At an initial size of 50 megawatt, the project was never going to be a linchpin in the company’s pipeline – which stood at 1,370 megawatt of active and contracted capacity as of the end of August. Yet it serves as another reminder that large-scale ambitions aren’t easily translated into physical infrastructure. That gives prospective investors another reason to approach the company's forthcoming New York listing – and its mooted valuation of $30 billion – with fresh scepticism.

The company’s filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission spells out that it intends to funnel proceeds of the initial public offering towards data centre projects and deployments. The document also makes clear that the group has yet to secure binding financing commitments for the buildout required under its agreements with Anthropic, the AI lab which is its other large customer. Debt markets are growing uneasy about neoclouds’ ability to follow through with the buildout that their future earnings depend on. Even a minor hitch lends credibility to the bear case.

CEO Hock Tan helped to jumpstart last week’s AI selloff by stating that access to capital could be a major constraint on the technology’s rollout. Nscale’s woes prove that server farms face obstacles on the ground, too.
Follow Jennifer Johnson on Bluesky and LinkedIn.

Microsoft has pulled out of a deal with London-based AI cloud provider Nscale that would have seen it rent computing capacity from a planned data centre in Loughton, Essex, the UK-based company said on October 18. Britain’s Telegraph newspaper first reported on the termination.
According to the Telegraph, national power grid officials had told Nscale they did not expect a power supply for the facility until the 2030s.

"Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and ​this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on ​our other contracts," an Nscale spokesperson told Reuters. The company said it is exploring alternative power sources for the site.
